system_description.narrative_title: Energy shocks, great‑power friction, and financial market stress
system_description.narrative_summary: The global order is an open, tightly coupled system in which renewed Middle East hostilities and maritime attacks around the Strait of Hormuz are driving energy-price shocks that ripple through inflation expectations and bond markets. Concurrently, great‑power competition (U.S., China, Russia) is reshaping alliances, commodity deals (notably U.S. engagement with Venezuela) and regional security dynamics, while technological and monetary policy shifts amplify systemic sensitivity. These interacting processes — energy supply risk, military escalation, capital‑market volatility, and strategic competition over critical tech and supply chains — create feedback loops that make the system highly reactive and hard to stabilise.
system_description.scope: International political, security and economic interactions: interstate conflicts and military strikes, energy production and maritime transit, global financial and bond markets, central‑bank and fiscal responses, strategic commodity deals, tech and supply‑chain competition (AI, semiconductors), and key non‑state actors and firms affecting those domains.
system_description.super_system: The globalized international political‑economic‑ecological system (the world order in which states, markets, technology and the environment interact).
adjacent_subsystems: International energy markets and maritime commerce (oil, LNG, Strait of Hormuz transit)
Global financial and monetary system (bond markets, central banks, inflation dynamics)
Great‑power strategic competition and alliance networks (US, China, Russia, regional partners)
Global technology and supply chains (AI governance, semiconductors, trade and investment flows)

variables.name: U.S.–Iran Gulf escalation
variables.description: The United States and Iran are trading strikes, mine and tanker incidents in and around the Gulf that are shifting local military control and raising the risk of wider regional confrontation.

variables.name: Russia–Ukraine high-intensity war
variables.description: Russia and Ukraine remain locked in an intensified, multi-domain war of drones, missiles and ground operations that is altering front lines, logistics and patterns of Western military and economic support.

variables.name: U.S.–China strategic rivalry
variables.description: The United States and China are competing across technology, trade and influence—notably over semiconductors, AI governance and Taiwan‑related security—reshaping supply chains and diplomatic alignments.

variables.name: Global oil supply reordering
variables.description: Major producers and consumers, including the United States, Venezuela, Saudi Arabia and Russia, are renegotiating production, access and commercial arrangements that are shifting sources of crude supply and long‑term industry partnerships.

variables.name: Global bond market repricing
variables.description: Global central banks (anchored by the U.S. Federal Reserve, ECB and BOJ) and investors are undergoing a rapid repricing of long‑term interest rates and risk premia as policy stances tighten and inflation expectations shift, altering capital flows and sovereign financing costs.
